title: Word Counter
story: You're analyzing a famous speech: 'I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up.' Which words appear most often? How many unique words are there? You need to count every word in the sentence and tally the results.
why: Word counting is the classic Map pattern — for each word, check if it's in the Map; if yes, increment; if no, insert with count 1.
analogy: A word counter is like a tally sheet at a polling station. As each vote (word) comes in, you look for the candidate's (word's) row. If you find it, you add a tally mark. If you don't, you create a new row with one tally. At the end, each row shows how many votes that candidate got.
try_it: Count letters instead of words: feed a string character by character into a Map[Char,Int]. Find the most frequent word by tracking the max count while iterating. Add a stop-word filter: words like 'the', 'a', 'and' are ignored and not counted.
tips: The get-then-insert pattern is the most common Map algorithm — memorize it: get → match → insert with updated value
Use a Vec to hold the words you want to report on — Map doesn't track which keys you've inserted in order
The first time you see a word, get returns None — insert(word, 1) to start the count
common_mistakes: Forgetting to start the count at 1 for new words — inserting with 0 gives wrong totals
Using `counts.insert(word, counts.get(word) + 1)` without matching — `.get()` returns Option, not Int
Only counting words that already exist — the None case (new word) must also be handled
